title: Paired conjunctions: both … and, not only … but also
tagline: Two-part linkers balance two ideas — keep them parallel, and invert after a fronted 'Not only'.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze: the second half of the pair is a classic gap
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Writing Part 1 — essay: balancing two arguments in one sentence
Speaking Part 3 — collaborative task: weighing up options
why: Pairs such as both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also and whether … or let a C1 writer set two ideas side by side in one tidy sentence. They are a favourite in open cloze, where you supply the missing half, and in transformations, where Not only forces inversion. Examiners also reward the discipline behind them: the two halves must be the same kind of phrase, and the verb must agree with the right subject.

branches.label: not only … but (also)
items: not only late but also rude

diagrams.title: Not only: inversion

before.text: Nadia not only won the debate, but she also broke the school record.

after.text: Not only did Nadia win the debate, but she also broke the school record.

steps: Move Not only to the front of the sentence.
Invert the auxiliary and the subject: did Nadia win (add do/does/did if the verb has no auxiliary).
Keep the second clause normal: but she also broke — no inversion after but.

diagrams.title: Which subject does the verb agree with?

rows.label: either … or
cells: Either Liam or his parents are coming.

rows.label: neither … nor
cells: Neither the players nor the coach was ready.

rows.label: not only … but also
cells: Not only the pupils but also the teacher was late.

head: Pair
Meaning
Example
rows: The trip was both exhausting and unforgettable.
You can either hand it in today or email it tomorrow.
Mateo has neither a laptop nor a tablet at home.
She is not only a gifted musician but also a fine coach.
Not only did the hotel lose our booking, but it also refused a refund.
two possibilities, both lead to the same result
Whether it rains or the sun shines, the match goes ahead.

use.point: both … and, either … or, neither … nor with nouns, verbs and adjectives

examples.text: The new library is both spacious and remarkably quiet.
Students may either submit a written report or give a short presentation.
examples.note: either + noun phrase or noun phrase: a choice
neither + verb nor verb: the verb after neither takes no negative

use.point: Not only … but also, and inversion after a fronted Not only

examples.text: Sofia is not only the captain but also the top scorer.
examples.note: no inversion when Not only follows the verb

examples.text: Not only did Mateo forget his notes, but he also left his phone on the bus.
Not only is the museum free, but it is also open until ten.

use.point: whether … or and agreement with the nearer subject

examples.text: Whether you agree or not, the decision stands.
examples.note: or not = two possibilities, same outcome

examples.text: Neither the coach nor the players were expecting such a result.
examples.note: plural players, the nearer subject, takes were

use.point: Parallel structure: the same kind of phrase on both sides

examples.text: The course taught us both how to research and how to present our findings.
examples.note: how to … and how to …: matching clauses

examples.text: She is determined either to win or to learn something from losing.

watch_out.wrong: Not only Mateo forgot his notes, but he also lost his phone.
watch_out.right: Not only did Mateo forget his notes, but he also lost his phone.
watch_out.why: A fronted Not only needs inversion with an auxiliary, as after any negative adverbial.

watch_out.wrong: Not only did she wins the prize, but she also gave a speech.
watch_out.right: Not only did she win the prize, but she also gave a speech.
watch_out.why: After the auxiliary did the main verb returns to its base form.

watch_out.wrong: He didn't neither call nor write.
watch_out.why: Neither … nor is already negative: do not add not.

watch_out.wrong: You can either to apply online or by post.
watch_out.right: You can either apply online or apply by post.
watch_out.why: Both halves must match: verb and verb, not verb and noun phrase.

watch_out.wrong: Neither the manager nor the staff was told.
watch_out.right: Neither the manager nor the staff were told.
watch_out.why: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, the staff, which is plural here.

watch_out.wrong: The film was both boring and it lasted too long.
watch_out.right: The film was both boring and too long.
watch_out.why: Parallel structure: adjective and adjective, not an adjective and a clause.

dialogue.title: Choosing the final-year project
dialogue.context: Sofia, Liam and Nadia are choosing a topic for their joint project, and Miss Vega drops by with advice.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: We have two options: the bridge-building challenge or the wildlife survey. Either we pick one now or we ask Miss Vega.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: The survey is not only more original but also far easier to finish on time.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Not only does it need less equipment, but it also lets us work outdoors.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I'm neither excited about the bridge nor convinced it's realistic.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Interesting. Both the survey and the bridge would work, but you need to choose.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Whether we choose the survey or the bridge, the deadline stays the same.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly. Neither the equipment nor the budget is a problem, so go for the project you believe in.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Then it's the survey. Not only did Liam persuade me, but he also found a free app for the data.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Agreed. We should both collect the data and analyse it together.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Perfect — either send me the plan on Friday or bring it to class on Monday.

items.sentence: Not only ___ the exam, but she also won a prize.
items.why: fronted Not only: auxiliary before the subject

items.sentence: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change.
items.why: agreement with the nearer subject: the students

items.sentence: Either Liam ___ Sofia will present first.
I can't decide whether to accept the offer ___ keep looking.
He neither called ___ left a message.
Not only the players but also the coach ___ delighted.
items.why: the nearer subject, the coach, is singular

items.sentence: The report was ___ clear but also persuasive.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the missing word or words. Where a verb is in brackets, use the correct form.

items.sentence: Not only ___ (Mateo/forget) his homework, but he also lost his bag.
Neither the coach ___ the players had expected such a result.
Both Sofia ___ Nadia applied for the exchange programme.
Either the manager or the assistants ___ (be) responsible for the error.
___ you agree or not, the decision is final.
She is not only a gifted musician but ___ a talented painter.
He wants to either study abroad ___ start work immediately.
Not only ___ (be/the museum) free, but it was also open late.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Sofia plays the violin and she also composes her own music.
items.second_end: the violin but she also composes her own music.

items.first: Liam didn't know the answer, and Mateo didn't either.
We can meet on Friday or on Saturday; I don't mind which.
It does not matter if it rains or not; the match will go ahead.
The film was long and it was also confusing.
Mateo did not phone Sofia, and he did not text her either.

summary: Use both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also and whether … or to balance two ideas in one sentence.
Keep the structure parallel: the same type of phrase must follow each half of the pair.
With either … or, neither … nor and not only … but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
Neither … nor is already negative; never add not to the verb.
A fronted Not only triggers inversion in the first clause only: Not only did she win, but she also ….
